E0767.summary: A riddle Atwood cites to illustrate the circulation of all things in all, and whose ‘omnia in omnibus’ she identifies with the Universal Ether.
E0767.body: Atwood cites the Hermetic Riddle to illustrate the circulation by which the Flower of Intellect is manifested back to its Archetypal Source: “The First all things in all gave the First Second all things in all, from the all in the First Second to the Third all” [IV.2 ¶20]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) its “omnia in omnibus” is identified with the Universal Ether [APP ¶119].

E0768.summary: Atwood's name for the art the book investigates: an ancient eastern tradition, peculiar and distinct from other philosophy, experimental and practical, embracing physical and moral science.
E0768.body:
In Atwood's own voice, the Hermetic tradition is ancient and eastern: “The Hermetic tradition opens early with the morning dawn in the eastern world. All pertaining thereto is romantic and mystical.” [I.1 ¶2]; it survives in dark and enigmatical monuments, emblems and writings. It is not bound to any one creed or class: “men of every religion, time and country and occupation, have been found professing it” [I.1 ¶31].

She treats it as a discipline of its own, “peculiar and distinct from every other branch of philosophy” [III.4 ¶2], requiring a naturally fitted disposition in its student. It is eminently experimental and practical in its consequences, and — with a hedge on its validity — “the Hermetic Science, supposing this indeed to be well founded, would include both in the ample compass of its experiment” [IV.4 ¶11], that is, both physical and moral science.

E0769.summary: In a Scholiast quoted by Atwood, the exact sealing of the philosophic vessel's orifices and junctures so no vapour escapes; equated with the lutum Sapientiae.
E0769.body: A Scholiast quoted in a footnote describes “how the orifices and junctures of the philosophic vessel must be encircled, so that no breath may go forth” [I.3 n57]. The same note equates the seal with the lutum Sapientiae: “with the lutum Sapientiae, or Hermetic seal” [I.3 n57]. Any plain meaning beyond the closing of the vessel is not given in this record.

E0770.summary: In the Appendix, the vehicle of the dead Divine Life within us, and at the same time the death of itself.
E0770.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The Hermetic sepulcher is the vehicle of the dead Divine Life within us” [APP ¶19], adding that it is at the same time the death of itself.

E0771.summary: The single repeated operation that comprises all the named operations (calcination, inceration, fixation, etc.), improving the matter each time; not ordinary chemical sublimation.
E0771.body: Atwood explains that Hermetic sublimation is the one operation covering all the named ones — calcination, inceration, fixation and the rest. It is repeated many times, and each repetition changes and improves the matter. She warns against the chemical reading: “This sublimation is not, therefore, exactly to be conceived by analogy with the ordinary chemical process, which is a mere elevation of the subject to the top of the vessel” [I.3 n14].

E0772.summary: The body of tradition Atwood says she has run cursorily through in the book.
E0772.body: Atwood refers to the Hermetic Tradition as the body of tradition she has run cursorily through [IV.4 ¶10].

E0773.summary: A work cited in the Appendix whose latter part illustrates the sacrifice of the first-fruits.
E0773.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the latter part of The Hermetic Wedding is cited as illustrating the sacrifice of the first-fruits [APP ¶74].

E0774.summary: A work Atwood cites in support of the Stone being prepared with the Lunar Vulcan, which she glosses as the first prepared Subject.
E0774.body: Atwood cites the Hermetical Triumph in support: it speaks of “the Stone of Philosophers, which is a pure petrification of the Spirit” [IV.1 ¶29], prepared with the Lunar Vulcan, which Atwood glosses as the first prepared Subject.

E0775.summary: A group voice cited and endorsed in the Appendix: the Mystery is discovered by artificial dissolution of the natural bond of life and regeneration under a reversed law.
E0775.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood endorses the Hermeticists' view that the Mystery is discovered by an artificial dissolution of the natural bond of life, and by regeneration under a reversed law [APP ¶7].

E0776.summary: In the Appendix, the magnetism of Light according to its own law, that Law being its emanating spirit, called wisdom.
E0776.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood defines it: “Hermetism is the magnetism of Light according to its own law” [APP ¶47]; that Law is its emanating spirit, called wisdom. Hermetism is thus identified with the magnetism of Light.

E0777.summary: An author cited in support of the existence and nature of a divine water of the chemists.
E0777.body: Atwood cites Hermolaus Barbarus, in a corollary to Dioscorus or some other work (the text is uncertain), in support of the divine water: “There is a celestial, or rather a divine water of the chemists” [I.1 ¶20].

E0778.summary: Historian cited for recording Egypt's remaining splendour after Cambyses.
E0778.body: Atwood names Herodotus as the historian who recorded the splendour that remained in Egypt after Cambyses [I.1 ¶10].

E0779.summary: Something of ‘illimitable virtue’ that Power and Motive corrects, educates, tames and directs; not further explained.
E0779.body: Atwood speaks of Power and Motive that “corrects and educates the Heroic Fire, tames and directs its illimitable virtue” [IV.1 ¶33]. The text gives no further explanation of the term here.

E0780.summary: The intellect whose long labors must all be passed through before the work is complete.
E0780.body: Atwood says that before the work is complete there are “all the labors of that Heroic Intellect to be passed through” [II.2 ¶29].

E0781.summary: The self-sacrificing will, read in Achilles' ‘vindicative will’, that enters after the loss and stirs the bitter waters to recover the lost kingdom.
E0781.body: In her allegorical reading of the Iliad, Atwood writes that after the loss “the Heroic Will enters in, self-sacrificing, and stirs the bitter waters” [III.1 ¶30], to recover the lost kingdom; she connects it with Achilles' vindicative will.

E0782.summary: Poet whose theogony Atwood cites as ‘very regular and correct’ when compared with alchemical descriptions, and as accepted by ancient philosophers.
E0782.body: Atwood cites Hesiod's theogony (beginning “First of all existed Chaos” [III.3 ¶41]) in support, judging it, when compared with alchemical descriptions, very regular and correct, and noting that ancient philosophers accepted it [III.3 ¶41, III.3 ¶42, III.3 n28]. The Epic Cycle and The Weeks and the Days are also named in connection with him.

E0783.summary: Atwood's image for the three offspring or supernal benefits that Life brings forth and sacrifices at each passage from one form of perfection to another.
E0783.body: Atwood describes Life bringing forth, at each passage from one form of perfection to another, three offspring or supernal benefits, “as it were three Hesperian Apples of Gold” [III.4 ¶25], which it sacrifices in turn.

E0784.summary: That in which the whole mystery is comprehended; the philosophers found them out and increased them.
E0784.body: The whole mystery is said to be comprehended in the hidden elements; of the philosophers it is said “they themselves found out these hidden elements, and themselves increased them” [II.1 ¶14]. The voice is unclear from the record. Compare hidden Wisdom, which hides beneath these elements [I.3 ¶25].

E0785.summary: In Hermes as quoted, the hidden Wisdom that comprehends all the world's wisdoms; learning the Arts consists in discovering the hidden elements beneath which it hides.
E0785.body: Hermes, quoted by Atwood, says: “All the wisdoms of the world, O son, are comprehended in this my hidden Wisdom” [I.3 ¶25]. The learning of the Arts consists in discovering the hidden elements beneath which this Wisdom hides.

E0786.summary: The officiant of the inner temple who passed aspirants on; in Clemens Alexandrinus, the Lord himself, who seals and illuminates the adepts in the true mysteries.
E0786.body:
In Atwood's own usage the Hierophant is the officiant of the inner temple who passed the aspirants on: “the Hierophant of the inner temple” [II.3 ¶36].

Quoting Clemens Alexandrinus, she gives the term a spiritual sense: “it is the Lord himself who is the hierophant” [II.2 ¶5], who seals and illuminates the adept. The same point recurs from the Bishop of Alexandria: “It is the Lord himself who is the Hierophanta.” [IV.2 ¶16] — in the true mysteries the Lord seals the Adepts and illuminates them.

E0787.summary: A group whose atmosphere, Atwood says in the Appendix, opens the depths of St Paul, in contrast to the commentators.
E0787.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the atmosphere of the higher Mystics is said to open St Paul's depths, in contrast with the commentators [APP ¶118].

E0788.summary: Physician named via Pliny as illustrator of medicine; Atwood uses ‘the Night of Hippocrates’ and his figure as the divinely endowed healer to illustrate the Art.
E0788.body: Hippocrates is named, after Pliny, as the illustrator of medicine, contemporary with the magic of Democritus [I.1 ¶12]. Atwood uses the expression ‘the Night of Hippocrates’ to name the end of the destructive way [III.2 ¶28]. She also uses him to illustrate the divinely endowed physician who imparts healing to others [IV.3 ¶32, IV.3 ¶34].

E0789.summary: Unnamed biographer of Pythagoras, cited as reporting that Pythagoras healed and purified his followers' souls by divine arts.
E0789.body: Atwood cites Pythagoras' biographer as reporting that Pythagoras healed and purified the souls of his followers by divine arts [II.2 ¶11].

forms: his ingenious disciple (of Cornelius Agrippa; not named)
E0790.summary: An unnamed disciple of Cornelius Agrippa, cited for ‘more suggestive language’ on the work's sequence and for Agrippa's poverty after his failure.
E0790.body: Atwood cites Agrippa's unnamed “ingenious disciple” as expressing, in more suggestive language, the joining, siege and creature sequence of the work: “Take our two serpents, which are to be found everywhere on the face of the earth” [III.1 ¶50]. She cites him again on Agrippa's poverty resulting from his failure: “This was it, adds his disciple, that made his necessities so vigorous and his purse so weak” [IV.1 ¶36].

E0792.summary: Painter cited as a contrast: in ordinary arts the maker's moral state does not show in the product, unlike in Alchemy.
E0792.body: Atwood uses Holbein as a contrast: “The pictures, of Holbein are not less beautiful for all the covetous spirit that reigned with their conception” [III.4 ¶8]. In ordinary arts the maker's moral state does not appear in the product; in Alchemy, by implication, it does.

E0793.summary: Scripture, cited as read by the Kabalists as divine symbols.
E0793.body: Atwood cites Holy Writ (the Pentateuch, the Old Testament) as read by the Kabalists as divine symbols [II.1 ¶40, II.1 ¶41].

E0794.summary: Poet whose Iliad and Odyssey Atwood reads as allegories of the Art, holding in the Appendix that the Hermetic is the only true key to them.
E0794.body:
Atwood reads Homer allegorically throughout. From the thirteenth book of the Odyssey she takes the cave in Ithaca with its two gates — “A lofty gate unfolds on either side” [II.4 ¶5] — as an allegory of descent and ascent [II.4 ¶5, II.4 ¶6, II.4 ¶7]. From the Iliad she reads Achilles' armour, the death of Patroclus, and Achilles' vow and death as an allegory of the Art [III.1 ¶25, III.1 ¶29, III.1 ¶30, III.1 n32, III.1 n35]. From Odyssey book 19 she cites in support that quietude and the cessation of mental energy are needed to receive divinity: “Be silent, repress your intellect, and do not speak.” [IV.2 ¶33, IV.2 n22].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) she states that the Hermetic is the only true key to the Iliad and Odyssey [APP ¶157], and identifies Proteus' last subterfuge, his transformation into a tree, with the tree of the Golden Bough, illustrating the elusive Protean life [APP ¶171].

E0795.summary: Nature of the same kind, which the perfected Spirit draws everywhere into itself.
E0795.body: Atwood describes the perfected Spirit as drawing “the Homogeneal Nature everywhere into itself” [IV.3 ¶29] — apparently, nature of its own kind.

E0796.summary: The one uniform substance in nature that is the material basis of Hermetic philosophy and sole principle of transmutation, life, increase and perfection.
E0796.body: Atwood posits “the existence of a Homogeneal Subject in nature” [I.2 ¶49]: one uniform substance that is the material basis of Hermetic philosophy and the sole principle of transmutation, life, increase and perfection.

forms: Hone soit qui mal y pense
E0797.summary: An unattributed motto Atwood invokes in support of her point against the charge of impiety.
E0797.body: Atwood invokes, in support of her point against the charge of impiety, the unattributed motto “Hone soit qui mal y pense.” [IV.4 ¶24]. Translation (ours): shamed be he who thinks evil of it.
